subject: physics

items.q: Rays of light travelling parallel to the principal axis pass into a convex lens. What happens to these rays?
items.correct: They are refracted and brought to a focus at the principal focus
items.misconception: They are reflected from the front face of the lens to a point
items.why: Lenses and mirrors are taught in the same topic, both are smooth and shiny, and both give images described as real or virtual, so the mechanism learned for mirrors is transferred to the lens. The specification is explicit: a lens forms an image by refracting light. The light goes through the lens and changes direction at each surface. A little light does reflect from the surfaces, but that is not how the image is made.
items.random_wrong: They are refracted and cross each other at the focal length

items.q: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?
items.correct: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
items.misconception: The distance from the lens to the object being viewed
items.why: Everyday camera language says you 'focus on' an object, so the distance out to the object is taken to be the focal length; focusing is heard as something done to the object rather than to the light. The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus, the point where rays arriving parallel to the axis are brought together. It belongs to the lens, not to the scene: the object can sit at any distance, and moving it does not change the focal length.
items.random_wrong: The distance from the lens to the sharp image

items.q: A convex lens forms an image of a distant tree on a screen. Where does the light change direction?
items.correct: As it enters the lens and again as it leaves
items.misconception: Only at the surface where the light leaves the lens
items.why: Ray diagrams draw a single bend at the lens line for simplicity, and refraction is often first taught with one boundary, so a second change of direction is not expected. A lens has two surfaces and the light is refracted at both. The single bend drawn at the lens line in a ray diagram is a shorthand for the two refractions that actually take place.
items.random_wrong: At the shiny front face, where light is reflected

items.q: Which statement about the image formed by a concave lens is always true?
items.correct: It is virtual, wherever the object is
items.misconception: It is real if the object is far enough away
items.why: Students learn that a convex lens gives a real image of a distant object and assume the same rule applies to any lens once the object is far enough away. A concave lens spreads light out, so the rays leaving it never meet. They only appear to come from a point on the object side, so the image is always virtual and can never be caught on a screen.
items.random_wrong: It is inverted, like the image from a lens

items.q: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus, as in a magnifying glass. What sort of image is formed?
items.correct: A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
items.misconception: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
items.why: Nearly all classroom work with a convex lens uses an object beyond the principal focus, which does give a real inverted image, so that case is taken to be the only one. When the object is closer to the lens than the principal focus, the rays leaving the lens are still spreading out and the image is virtual, upright and magnified, as in a magnifying glass.
items.random_wrong: A virtual image, upright but smaller than it

items.q: How can you tell that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?
items.correct: It can be caught on a screen put where it forms
items.misconception: It appears the same way up as the object does
items.why: Real is heard as meaning true to life, so an image that looks correct is called real and an upside-down one is called false. Real and virtual describe whether the rays actually meet, not how the image looks. Whether it can be caught on a screen is the test, and a real image from a lens comes out inverted.
items.random_wrong: It can be seen by looking through the lens

items.q: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?
items.correct: It carries straight on, with no change of direction
items.misconception: It is bent so that it passes through the principal focus
items.why: Students learn that a lens refracts light and apply that to all rays equally, without noticing that the two surfaces are parallel at the centre so the direction is unchanged. At the centre the two faces of the lens are effectively parallel, so a ray passing through there emerges travelling in its original direction. It is drawn as a straight line through the centre.
items.random_wrong: It is curved to follow the two faces of the lens

items.q: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?
items.correct: Spreading away from the principal axis
items.misconception: Bending in to reach the principal focus beyond
items.why: The convex rule is learned first and is applied to the concave diagram without change, because both lenses are drawn with a principal focus marked. A concave lens diverges the light. The refracted ray travels away from the axis, and only the dashed line traced backwards passes through the principal focus, which lies on the object side.
items.random_wrong: Carrying straight on to the far side of it

items.q: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and for a concave lens, using the same object in each. Which feature is the same in both diagrams?
items.correct: The ray through the centre of the lens is undeviated
items.misconception: Both images are turned upside down compared with the object
items.why: The first image a student meets is the real inverted image from a convex lens, and inversion becomes attached to the idea of a lens rather than to that particular case. Rays through a concave lens are spread out and traced back to a point above the axis on the object side, so the image comes out upright, smaller and virtual every time.
items.random_wrong: Both images can be caught on a screen behind

items.q: Which two quantities are needed to calculate the magnification produced by a lens?
items.correct: The height of the image and the object height
items.misconception: The focal length of the lens and the object height
items.why: The word focus is used both for the special point and for a sharp image, and the only ray diagram many students remember is the one for a very distant object, where the image really does form at the principal focus. The principal focus only tells you where rays parallel to the axis are brought together. Rays from a nearby object are not parallel, so they cross somewhere else, and that is where the image forms.
items.random_wrong: The distance to the image and to the object

items.q: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?
items.correct: 3, from 15 mm divided by 5 mm
items.misconception: 0.33, from 5 mm divided by 15 mm
items.why: The object comes first in the story of what happens, and in the phrase object and image, so it is put first in the fraction as well. The specification gives magnification = (image height)/(object height). The image height goes on top, so an image larger than the object gives a magnification greater than 1.
items.random_wrong: 3 mm, as the heights were in mm

items.q: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?
items.correct: 0.30, as the image is smaller
items.misconception: 3.3, since 8.0 is divided by 2.4
items.why: The object comes first in the story of what happens, and in the phrase object and image, so it is put first in the fraction as well. The specification gives magnification = (image height)/(object height). The image height goes on top, so an image larger than the object gives a magnification greater than 1.

items.q: A student measures both heights in centimetres and calculates a magnification of 2.5. How should this answer be written?
items.correct: As 2.5 on its own, because a ratio has no units at all
items.misconception: As 2.5 cm, keeping the unit of the heights measured
items.why: Students are trained to carry a unit through every calculation and to lose marks for leaving one out, so they attach the unit of the measurements they started with. Dividing a height by a height cancels the unit: cm divided by cm leaves a plain number. A magnification is written as a bare number such as 3 or 0.30.
items.random_wrong: As 2.5 mm, since mm is a unit used for heights

items.q: An object is 4.0 cm tall and its image is 60 mm tall. What must be done before the magnification equation is used?
items.correct: Convert one height so that both are in the same unit
items.misconception: Nothing at all, since a magnification has no unit anyway
items.why: The rule that magnification has no unit is remembered as meaning that units do not matter anywhere in the calculation. The unit only cancels if it is the same on the top and the bottom. Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm, so convert one of them first.
items.random_wrong: Divide the two heights just as they are given

items.q: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?
items.correct: A vertical line with outward arrowheads at each end
items.misconception: A vertical line with two arrowheads pointing inwards
items.why: Students try to make the symbol describe what the lens does to light rather than remembering that it records the shape of the lens. The arrowheads follow the shape, not the action. A convex lens bulges outwards, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is hollowed inwards, so its arrowheads point inwards.
items.random_wrong: A shape drawn curved outwards on each of its two faces

items.q: Which symbol is used in a ray diagram to represent a concave lens?
items.correct: A line with inward arrowheads at both ends
items.misconception: A line with arrowheads pointing outwards at both ends
items.why: Students try to make the symbol describe what the lens does to light rather than remembering that it records the shape of the lens. The arrowheads follow the shape, not the action. A convex lens bulges outwards, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is hollowed inwards, so its arrowheads point inwards.
items.random_wrong: A line drawn thinner in the middle than at the edges

items.q: Is the focal length the distance from the lens to the image?
items.correct: The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus.
items.misconception: The focal length is however far the image happens to be from the lens, so it changes when the object is moved.
items.why: In practical work students measure the lens-to-screen distance when the image is sharp, and for a very distant object that distance really is the focal length, so the special case is remembered as the definition. The principal focus is where rays that arrive parallel to the principal axis are brought to a focus. The focal length is the fixed distance from the lens to that point, and it does not change when the object is moved.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does virtual mean that the image cannot be seen?
items.correct: A virtual image can be seen by looking through the lens; it simply cannot be caught on a screen.
items.misconception: A virtual image is one that cannot be seen at all, so any image you can actually look at must be real.
items.why: In everyday speech virtual suggests something not really there, so students read it as invisible rather than as a statement about where the rays actually go. Virtual describes the rays, not the viewer. The rays only appear to come from the image position, so no screen catches it, but the eye can still see it by looking through the lens.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must a magnification be greater than 1?
items.correct: No. A magnification less than 1 means the image is smaller than the object.
items.misconception: Magnification means making something bigger, so the answer must always come out greater than 1.
items.why: The everyday meaning of magnify is to enlarge, so an answer such as 0.30 looks like a mistake and gets turned upside down to give 3.3. In physics magnification is just the ratio of image height to object height. If the image is smaller the ratio is less than 1, and that is the correct answer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should a ray diagram show the true curved shape of the lens?
items.correct: No. The lens is drawn as a single vertical line with arrowheads at its ends.
items.misconception: A ray diagram should show the lens as it really looks, curved on both faces, with the rays bending at each curved surface.
items.why: Students are told the lens works because of its curved surfaces, so they assume the diagram must show them, and textbook photographs reinforce the picture. In ray diagrams the lens is represented by a straight line with arrowheads, and all the bending is drawn happening at that line. The symbol records the type of lens, not its true shape.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a virtual image always smaller than the object?
items.correct: No. A convex lens can form a virtual image that is larger than the object.
items.misconception: Virtual means the image is not properly there, so it is always a small, faint copy of the object.
items.why: The virtual image students meet most often is the diminished one from a concave lens, and the word virtual suggests something weaker than the real thing. Virtual says only that the rays appear to come from the image. A magnifying glass gives a virtual image that is upright and larger than the object.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the focal length something you could measure with a ruler held against the glass of the lens?
items.correct: No. The focal length is measured from the lens out to the principal focus, not across the glass itself.
items.misconception: The focal length is a measurement of the lens itself, such as how thick the glass is at its widest point.
items.why: The phrase 'focal length of the lens' sounds like a dimension belonging to the lens, and students have seen that fatter, more curved lenses behave differently, so the length is looked for on the glass itself. The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus - the point where rays parallel to the axis are brought together. It is measured in the space beyond the lens. A thicker, more strongly curved lens does have a shorter focal length, but the thickness of the glass is not the focal length.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: An object is 5 mm tall and its image is 15 mm tall. Do you find the magnification by subtracting the heights?
items.correct: No. Magnification = image height divided by object height = 15 mm / 5 mm = 3.
items.misconception: Magnification is how much bigger the image is than the object, found by taking the object height away from the image height.
items.why: In everyday arithmetic 'how much bigger' is answered by a difference, so the two heights are compared by subtracting instead of dividing - additive reasoning used where a ratio is needed. Magnification compares the two sizes as a ratio, not a difference: magnification = image height / object height. Here 15 mm / 5 mm = 3, meaning the image is 3 times as tall as the object. Because it is a ratio of two lengths, magnification has no units.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
